intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-43 (MRT43) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the WASHC4 gene (615748) on chromosome 12q23.3.

checks.evidence_quote: a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP [Strumpellin and WASH (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and scar homolog)-interacting protein] gene
checks.explanation: The abstract supports a SWIP change as the cause of ARID in one consanguineous family. It does not name MRT43, does not state that the change is homozygous, and does not mention compound heterozygous mutations; those details likely come from other papers.

checks.evidence_quote: In 2011, KIAA1033/WASHC4 was associated with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID)

paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-43 (MRT43) is an intellectual disability disorder that was first described as nonsyndromic (Ropers et al., 2011). Later reports described syndromic forms with dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, macrocephaly or microcephaly, and skeletal muscle involvement (Assoum et al., 2020; Gangfuß et al., 2022). Motor symptoms have also been reported, including clumsiness, fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria (Courtland et al., 2021).

checks.claim: MRT43 is an intellectual disability disorder that was first described as nonsyndromic.
checks.evidence_quote: Identification of a novel candidate gene for non-syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability: the WASH complex member SWIP.
checks.explanation: The title describes the disorder as non-syndromic. This is the original report.

checks.claim: Later reports described syndromic forms of MRT43 with dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, macrocephaly or microcephaly, and skeletal muscle involvement.
checks.evidence_quote: Both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules.
checks.explanation: Dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, macrocephaly and microcephaly are reported. Skeletal muscle involvement is not mentioned in this abstract.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from 7 children who had been evaluated at the Royal Hospital in Muscat, Oman. The children were homozygous for the WASHC4 c.3056C-G mutation, and Courtland et al. (2021) stated that they had originally been reported by Ropers et al. (2011). Developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary reason for medical evaluation. However, all patients also had motor symptoms at a mean age of 10.4 years. Their movements were described as 'clumsy', and clinical examination showed fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. By the time of recent communication with the parents, the patients were an average of 21 years old, and their symptoms had not notably worsened. The authors suggested that their mouse model either differs from the human patients or may predict future disease progression in these individuals. The mice worsened significantly at 5 to 6 months of age, which was thought to be equivalent to about 30 to 35 human years.

paragraphs.text: Ropers et al. (2011) studied affected members of a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability. In them, the authors found a nonsynonymous sequence change in the SWIP (WASHC4) gene, which encodes a member of the WASH complex. After SNP filtering, this was one of only 2 remaining changes. The authors considered it causative based on high pathogenicity and evolutionary conservation scores and on functional considerations. In functional studies, the mutation significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) studied the autosomal recessive WASHC4 mutation c.3056C-G (P1019R). They stated that Ropers et al. (2011) had previously identified this mutation in a cohort of children with nonsyndromic intellectual disability. They noted that the affected residue lies in a region of SWIP thought to be critical for binding the WASH component Strumpellin. In coimmunoprecipitation studies in HEK cells, mutant SWIP pulled down significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wildtype SWIP (54.8% and 41.4% of wildtype, respectively). This indicated that the mutation hinders WASH complex formation.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) defined the neuronal WASH complex proteome using in vivo BioID in mouse brain, with a WASH1-BioID2 probe expressed under the human synapsin-1 promoter. They identified 175 significantly enriched proteins (fold-change of 4 or more, FDR less than 0.05). These included all 5 WASH complex subunits and 13 previously reported WASH interactors, as well as endosomal, endocytic, cytoskeletal, and excitatory postsynaptic proteins. These results supported a major endosomal trafficking role for WASH in mouse brain. Courtland et al. (2021) proposed that WASH complex destabilization caused by the P1019R mutation drives cognitive and motor impairments through endolysosomal dysfunction in the brain. Over time, this dysfunction led to accumulation of neurodegenerative markers, including upregulation of unfolded protein response modulators and lysosomal enzymes, lipofuscin buildup, and cleaved caspase-3.

paragraphs.text: Gangfuß et al. (2022) performed proteomic profiling of fibroblasts from a WASHC4-deficient patient and found dysregulation of proteins relevant for maintaining the neuromuscular axis. Immunostaining of a muscle biopsy from the same patient confirmed dysregulation of proteins needed for proper muscle function. The authors stated that histologic studies and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopy supported a role for WASHC4 in protein processing and clearance in humans.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) used CRISPR to generate a knockin mouse carrying a CCT-to-CGT point mutation in exon 29 of the mouse Washc4 gene. This mutation mimics the human WASHC4 c.3056C-G (P1019R) mutation. On Western blot of adult whole-brain lysate from homozygous mutant mice, the WASH complex members Strumpellin (3.8% of wildtype) and WASH1 (1.1% of wildtype) were almost completely lost. This phenocopied data from the human patients and indicated that the WASH complex is unstable in vivo.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) performed tandem-mass-tag spatial proteomics of brain from 10-month-old mutant mice. Four WASH proteins (WASHC1, WASHC2, WASHC4, and WASHC5) and RAB21A were differentially abundant in all 7 subcellular fractions, and 728 proteins differed overall between genotypes. An endosomal module (M38) containing WASH, CCC, Retriever, and CORVET-HOPS proteins was significantly decreased in mutant brain. A lysosomal module (M36) containing cathepsins, hydrolases, and progranulin was significantly increased. Cultured cortical neurons from homozygous mutant mice had enlarged somatic EEA1-positive early endosomes, with no change in puncta number. They also had fewer but larger cathepsin D-positive lysosomal puncta than wildtype neurons. These findings were consistent with a loss-of-function mutation causing morphologic abnormalities of the endolysosomal pathway.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) found significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining in the motor cortex of 10-month-old mutant mice (44.0% vs 25.4% of DAPI-positive nuclei), but not in adolescent mice. Transmission electron microscopy of motor cortex from 7-month-old mutant mice showed large electron-dense lipofuscin deposits. Dopaminergic cell number in the substantia nigra pars compacta and striatal dopaminergic innervation were unchanged. This suggested that the motor cortex was the main movement-related region affected.

paragraphs.text: In behavioral testing, Courtland et al. (2021) found that homozygous mutant mice performed normally in novel object recognition and Y-maze alternation. However, the mice showed a significant deficit in cued fear memory recall 48 hours after tone-footshock pairing, both at adolescence (P42) and in adulthood (6.5 months), while their responses to footshock and tones were intact. These results were consistent with the hypothesis that the P1019R mutation causes cognitive impairment in humans. The mutant mice also had an almost 50% reduction in rotarod retention time at both P45 and 5.5 months. TreadScan gait analysis was largely normal at adolescence. By 5.5 months, however, it showed significantly longer hindlimb swing times, longer stride lengths, and decreased homologous coupling, demonstrating progressive motor decline.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively analyzed 7 Omani children who were homozygous for a c.3056C-G transversion in the WASHC4 gene, resulting in a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution. Courtland et al. (2021) stated that these patients with MRT43 had originally been reported by Ropers et al. (2011). In addition to developmental delay or learning difficulties, all patients had motor symptoms, including clumsiness, fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. The affected residue lies in a region of SWIP thought to be critical for binding Strumpellin. In coimmunoprecipitation studies in HEK cells, mutant SWIP pulled down significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wildtype SWIP (54.8% and 41.4% of wildtype, respectively). In homozygous knockin mice carrying the equivalent mutation, Strumpellin and WASH1 were almost completely lost in brain lysate (3.8% and 1.1% of wildtype, respectively).
